summary:
Project Celestial Sparks started with a simple question has the flame actually extinguished We wanted to look past predicting whether a droplet fire goes out in space and think about what that means for fuel efficiency and preventing accidents in spacecraft.
Working with NASA's FLEX PSI 69 data from 274 microgravity combustion tests aboard the ISS 2009 to 2011 we read articles on Damkohler extinction theory flame blowout limits flammability maps and machine learning for combustion prediction. We wanted to dig deeper but ran into real constraints we could not download a 255 GB dataset and we only had about 3 to 4 days for research.
So we built what we could an interactive dashboard and flame extinction simulator that predicts whether methanol or n heptane droplets will go out based on test conditions. We trained a statistical model ported it to TypeScript so it runs directly in a browser and validated it against 274 reference probabilities. It is not a complete solution but it is an honest first step toward understanding when a flame truly dies in microgravity and why that matters for safer more efficient spaceflight.
That is what we did in a short amount of time. Hope that makes sense.
details:
(it uses a multinomial logistic regression trained on the 274 FLEX records, ported to TypeScript so it runs in the browser with no Python at runtime. Oxygen is the strongest predictor of extinction, followed by droplet size, and the model reproduces the recorded outcomes with an out-of-fold AUC of 0.85.)

OUR MAIN IDEA FOR RESEARCH WAS TO CHECK IF THE FLAME IS ACTUALLY EXTINGUISED AND HASN'T JUST DISAPPEARED.

(Though, due to lack of time (3-4 days of research and prep), we couldn't do much :/ )

What the project is: A research website with an interactive simulator that predicts whether a microgravity droplet flame will extinguish, based on NASA's FLEX PSI-69 experimental data (274 tests, methanol and n-heptane, ISS 2009–2011).

Tech stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, recharts (for the boundary chart), vitest + Testing Library (42 tests), ESLint. The model is a TypeScript port of a scikit-learn multinomial logistic regression — it reads an embedded JSON contract (coefficients, scaler stats, one-hot categories) so no Python or external model server is needed at runtime. It deploys to Vercel directly from GitHub.

What was used: The public NASA PSI-69 dataset release (DOI 10.60555/mbq8-0451), the Dietrich et al. (2015) FLEX methods report (NASA/TP-2015-216046), the Lecoustre et al. (2011) critical-Damköhler extinction theory, plus supporting combustion literature. Local project documents include the FLEX requirements document, test plan, engineering requirements document, and Declaration of Data.

How it was built: The analysis (physics, statistics, model training) was done separately in Python and exported as a JSON model contract. That contract was then ported 1:1 into TypeScript (lib/model.ts) so the site can make predictions client-side and through Next.js API routes (/api/predict, /api/boundary). The frontend was built with Next.js pages for the dashboard, simulator, paper, and references. Every claim in the model was pinned against the original Python results with a 274-row parity test (±0.001).

AI usage: An AI agent did the engineering work since we are not good at AI/ML and we started 3-4 days earlier, we used opencode to do stuff like cleaning the dataset, making audits, schemas and all. The research: the dataset interpretation, the findings, the statistics, the report, and the conclusions was done by the team. (we were specifically interested about how this question fascinated researchers in 2017 as well (the unpredictable nature of flame in microgravity), and how sensors failed 2/3 of the test)

How I got the idea: I wanted to take NASA's publicly released microgravity flame data and turn it into something cool: not just a static report/a model that predicts, but an interactive tool where someone could change conditions and see how the extinction boundary moves (we are using a 3 class verified model, that was created specifically after comparing with the relevant science facts, we aren't that good at science coz we are high schoolers, so we had to learn a lot). The FLEX dataset is a natural fit because it is well-documented, publicly available, and centers on an intuitive question: at what oxygen level does a flame stop burning in space? So yeah, we went ahead and built it (more like the research was done by us, the coding part was done by AI).

(btw we also planned on using how the flame is in the airflow to our advantage to optimize fuel efficency LOL, I mean in theory it can prove to be advantegous)
